messages:
acme-noc: Hey Redwood — since ~02:00 UTC we've had intermittent mTLS handshake failures from our VPC to the Private control plane in us-east-1. Thousands of app errors, looks like immediate TLS alerts

jana: thanks — can you paste the exact app error and a short tcpdump or openssl s_client output? also confirm the FQDN you're hitting (controlplane host)

acme-noc: app log: 'tls: handshake error: local error: tls: received alert: handshake failure'
TCPDUMP snippet we captured:
```
12:03:19.123456 IP 10.0.5.10.43210 > controlplane.private.redwood.com.443: Flags [S], seq 0, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 12345 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
12:03:19.234567 IP controlplane.private.redwood.com.443 > 10.0.5.10.43210: Flags [R.], seq 0, ack 1, win 0, length 0
# or we see: TLSv1.3 ClientHello, then TLSv1.3 Alert, fatal, handshake_failure
```

jana: ok. please run this from one of your affected hosts and paste output (remove any private keys):
```
openssl s_client -connect controlplane.private.redwood.com:443 -cert client.pem -key client.key -CAfile ca.pem -servername controlplane.private.redwood.com -tlsextdebug -status
```

acme-noc: ran that, result:
```
CONNECTED(00000003)
140736297462272:error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:sslv3 alert handshake failure:ssl/record/rec_layer_s3.c:1544:SSL alert number 40
---
read:errno=0
```

jana: thanks — two quick possibilities: (1) the client cert chain/key usage not acceptable to control plane (must include clientAuth EKU + full chain), (2) an egress middlebox/proxy is mangling ClientHello (SNI/ALPN/extension truncation) or truncating TLS record (MTU/NAT fragment).

eli: +1. also check NAT port mapping and ephemeral port reuse/timeouts. We've seen TCP RSTs when enterprise NAT rewrites source ports and our control plane rejects session resume or clientnonce. can you tcpdump with packet lengths to confirm ClientHello size? if the CH is split across IP fragments or TCP segments and your middlebox doesn't reassemble, handshake will fail.

acme-noc: here's the openssl -msg output we ran:
```
>>> TLS 1.3 Handshake [length 0141], ClientHello
>>> TLS 1.3 Alert [length 0002], fatal, handshake_failure
```

tom: can you also verify DNS resolution and SNI? sometimes corporate proxies rewrite DNS to an inspect appliance which terminates TLS and doesn't present the client cert to upstream. run:
```
nslookup controlplane.private.redwood.com
curl -v --resolve controlplane.private.redwood.com:443:34.55.66.77 https://controlplane.private.redwood.com/health --cacert ca.pem --cert client.pem --key client.key
```
(the IP used above is our control plane egress address; use the IP we give you in the ticket if you don't want DNS to be involved)

acme-noc: curious — our egress goes through a corporate NGFW that does TLS inspection. We do have OCSP/Stapling enabled. Could stapling break client auth?

jana: OCSP stapling itself shouldn't break client auth, but some inspection proxies strip TLS extensions or terminate and re-initiate TLS without forwarding client cert auth. If your NGFW is a TLS-terminator, the Redwood control plane will see the proxy as the client (and then expect a client cert from it) and the chain will fail.

eli: run a raw tcpdump to show whether the proxy is terminating TLS (look for two separate TLS sessions: one between host->proxy and proxy->controlplane). command:
```
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s0 -w /tmp/controlplane.pcap host controlplane.private.redwood.com and port 443
```
Upload the pcap to the ticket. If you can't share pcap, at minimum capture packet lengths and the source/dest IP pairs.

acme-noc: we captured and see two TLS sessions. proxy is terminating. We'll check with security team to disable inspection for that FQDN.

tom: additional checks on your firewall: ensure outbound allowlist keeps source port mapping stable and doesn't rewrite SNI. Example allowlist for Palo Alto (allow egress to control plane IPs over 443, NAT 'no-translation' for these flows):
```
# Palo Alto - example security policy
from: trust to: untrust service: application-https destination: 34.55.66.77/32 action: allow
# NAT rule: source translation: none (keep original source port) for traffic to 34.55.66.77
```
Or iptables example if you're running an egress gateway yourself:
```
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -d 34.55.66.77/32 -p tcp --dport 443 -j MASQUERADE --to-ports 1024-65535
# ensure conntrack timeout for ESTABLISHED is high enough: sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established=86400
```

acme-noc: giving this to our security team now. we can try bypassing the proxy as a repro step.

infra-bot: escalation created: E-7832 (Private Control Plane mTLS failures — suspected TLS inspection / NAT fragment). Ticket link: https://redwood.internal/tickets/E-7832

jana: thanks. if the proxy is unavoidable, an interim workaround is to terminate TLS at your egress and perform mutual TLS between your egress appliance and Redwood (i.e., have your appliance present a valid client cert). long term we recommend an allowlist exception for control plane FQDN/IPs.

acme-noc: one more Q — we use a cert with CN=acme-client and chain length 2. how can I validate EKU?

jana: run:
```
openssl x509 -in client.pem -text -noout | grep -A3 'X509v3 Extended Key Usage'
```
You should see 'TLS Web Client Authentication' or 'clientAuth'. If missing, generate a client cert with clientAuth EKU and full chain.

acme-noc: copy. we've opened an exception with security, capturing a full pcap for the ticket, will update once they disable inspection or provide a passthrough rule. thanks all :thumbsup:

jana: appreciate the quick repro info — keeping E-7832 assigned to network oncall. we'll follow up with the control plane team if we see failures after passthrough is enabled. :mag:
